title: Supply-side policy and the government's aims

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Trace the effects of supply-side measures on the government's macroeconomic aims - growth, employment, price stability and the external position - and weigh the trade-offs between them.

blocks.heading: Which aims the measures move
blocks.text: The macroeconomic aims are those of topic 4.2: growth in total output, employment, price stability and a sound external position. Supply-side measures tend to serve them through one channel: the economy's capacity to produce. A more productive workforce tends to mean more total output, so the growth aim is served. Workers who produce more tend to be easier to employ profitably, so the employment aim gains. Where the economy can produce more for the same effort, pressure on prices tends to ease, and a leaner cost base tends to make exports easier to sell abroad, serving the external position.

blocks.heading: A training programme traced to the aims
blocks.text: Suppose the government funds a welding course in Otavi, and 200 trainees raise their output per worker by a fifth. Mechanism: each trained worker produces more, so firms in Otavi can fill larger orders without taking on more machines; total output rises, serving growth. Because the trained welders generate more revenue per hour, firms tend to offer more hours and take on more of them, serving employment. Where local firms can quote lower prices from lower costs per unit, buyers gain and pressure on prices eases, serving price stability. Against this, the course costs public money now, while its gains build over years - the trade-off the government weighs.

blocks.heading: One measure, several aims, uneven gains
blocks.text: The gains land unevenly. A worker who gains a skill earns more and keeps a job more easily. A firm gains capacity and may cut its cost per unit. The government tends to gain on the aims of growth and employment but pays the cost now, and where it cuts direct taxes to sharpen incentives, it loses revenue, which may force public spending down. Consumers gain where lower costs lead to slower price rises. In Brazil, a large training institute widened gains across whole regions, but trainees far from the institutes waited years.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The aims themselves are defined in topic 4.2, the role of government in holding them in topic 4.1, and the fiscal and monetary routes to the same aims in topics 4.3 and 4.4.
